title: Redwood Discovery - Aether Payments latency & throughput
summary: Discovery call to understand Aether Payments' latency & throughput SLOs for real-time fraud and customer support workflows. Discussed p95 targets, concurrency, streaming, benchmarking plan, and tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Next steps: run benchmarks with Aether prompts, share Dedicated pricing and SOC2 docs, schedule infra deep-dive.
next_steps: Run 1k-request token/sec benchmark using Aether sample prompts (Liam to run; target 2026-03-09)
Schedule Private/VPC deep-dive with Aether infra (Liam + Evan) week of 2026-03-11
action_items: Maya: send pricing & SOC2 bundle by 2026-03-05
Liam: run token/sec benchmark and upload results to shared sheet by 2026-03-09
Evan: provide representative prompt set and QPS targets by 2026-03-06
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-03-04 | Start: 14:30 PST | Duration: 47m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Aether Head of ML), Sonia Rao (Aether CTO), Evan Li (Aether SRE)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um Liam our SE is on as well, quick agenda - understand your p95 latency targets, concurrency needs, streaming use cases, and decide whether Hosted / Dedicated / Private is the right fit.
[00:12] Carlos: hi thanks, yeah quick background: Aether runs fraud scoring + a live chat assistant; fraud is synchronous inline during auth (sub-300ms ideally) and chat needs streaming but low tail latency so customers feel real-time.
[00:28] Sonia: we tried a few hosted apis but tail spikes killed conversion; we want p95 below 350ms for fraud at our 99 req/s peak, and p95 below 800ms for chat streaming with per-user concurrency ~5.
[00:45] Liam: ok got it, so fraud path is single-turn short prompts, high QPS, tight p95. Chat is streaming with context up to 4k tokens and concurrent sessions. A couple of clarifying q's: what's your average prompt length and tokens/sec target on streaming?
[01:05] Carlos: average fraud prompt is ~120 tokens, model outputs ~60 tokens. Streaming target is ~30-50 tokens/sec perceived by user, internal token generation can be faster but we want smoothness.
[01:18] Evan: infra constraints: we run in us-west, VPC peering is possible, want audit logs into our SIEM, and KMS integration is a must. Also SSO + RBAC internally.
[01:32] Liam: our platform supports VPC + private control plane, KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs. For p95s, quick orientation: on Hosted we typically see p95s for short generation (up to 256 tokens) in the 80-200ms range for small/efficient models, but depends on model size and batching; Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower tail if you reserve capacity. Private gives you network control but deployment overhead.
[02:05] Sonia: can you give concrete numbers - like for a 2xA100 pool what's your p95 and tokens/sec?
[02:12] Liam: sure ballpark: for a 2xA100 equivalent pool serving a 7B-ish open model unquantized we often see sustained throughput ~1.2k-1.8k tokens/sec aggregate with p95 single-request latency ~120-300ms for 128-token generations. If you enable quantization and optimized kernels that can go up to ~3k-4k tokens/sec aggregate. But important: those numbers vary with concurrency and sequence lengths.
[02:37] Carlos: ok that seems promising. For fraud our reqs are tiny but we have high concurrency during peaks - 200 concurrent short requests. How does your autoscaling work and how do you control tail at 200 concurrency?
[02:52] Liam: we have autoscale policies for Dedicated: you can pin a min pool size and set scale-up thresholds by CPU/GPU utilization and queue length. For tail control we do a few things: continuous batching with strict latency SLOs (so we cap batching window for low-latency routes), prefix/KV cache for common prefixes, and model routing to cheaper/compatible variants under load. In practice if you want strict p95 under 300ms at 200 concurrency you'd reserve enough Dedicated capacity to keep average utilization lower - otherwise Hosted burst policies can spill to higher-latency nodes.
[03:28] Sonia: what's the cost tradeoff - reserved Dedicated vs hosted burst credits?
[03:32] Maya: Hosted is pay-as-you-go and good for variable traffic; Dedicated is monthly commit but gives predictable latency and reserved throughput, typically lowering unit cost at scale. We can run a cost model for your traffic - Liam can capture your QPS and token distribution and we can show the crossover point.
[03:50] Carlos: we have a monthly baseline of ~8M tokens for fraud and 12M tokens for chat, with peaks during Black Friday expected to be 4-5x baseline.
[04:03] Liam: ok we'll use those numbers for the cost/capacity model. For benchmarking, recommended plan: provide a representative prompt set and target concurrency; we'll run a 1k-request synthetic benchmark from our Dedicated/Hosted environments and capture p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec. We'll also do streaming latencies and observed token-per-second rates.
[04:25] Evan: how do you measure streaming perceived latency? We need stable inter-token gaps not a burst then long tail.
[04:31] Liam: good point - we capture time-to-first-byte (TTFB) and inter-token spacing; for streaming we can tune the chunk size and server-side flush frequency to smooth perceived rate. Our benchmarks include a simulated UI to measure perceived tokens/sec.
[04:46] Carlos: any caveats about KV cache and prefix caching for fraud? Our fraud prompts share a lot of structured fields so maybe heavy cache hit rates.
[04:55] Liam: that helps a lot. With prefix/KV caching you can reduce compute per request significantly; for very repetitive prompts cache hit rates of 60-80% can reduce p95 by 2-3x for cached requests. We'll want to analyze your prompt variability - Evan can share sample set.
[05:12] Sonia: security - we need SOC2, SAML SSO, customer-managed KMS where keys never leave our account. Are those supported?
[05:20] Maya: yes, we have SOC2 Type II, SAML/SSO, and for Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. For Dedicated we have KMS integrations and can put key material behind your KMS depending on setup. We'll attach our security pack.
[05:36] Evan: also need audit logs shipped to Splunk or Sumo - can we export logs?
[05:40] Liam: yes audit logs and request-level traces can be forwarded; there's an audit log export. We can provide an example config.
[05:48] Carlos: great. Ok more on benchmarking: we want p95 <= 250ms for fraud at 200 concurrency and p95 <= 800ms for streaming chat at 2k concurrent sessions? That second number might be off - we expect concurrency across chat to be more like 2k sessions but only a fraction are active at the same time - say 400 active generations.
[06:10] Liam: that's much more reasonable. 400 active concurrent generations with streaming is doable on Dedicated with appropriate pool sizing. For exact sizing we'll run the benchmark with your prompt set and scale up the pool until p95 meets target, then we can map to monthly committed capacity.
[06:27] Maya: I'll capture these target p95s in follow-up: fraud 250ms p95 @200 concurrency, chat streaming 800ms p95 @400 active generations, perceived 30-50 tokens/sec.
[06:38] Carlos: is there a recommended model family? We currently evaluate 7B and 13B open models; lower-latency for fraud could use distilled/few-shot tuned 7B and chat could use 13B for quality.
[06:51] Liam: yep typical pattern: use a small, fast model for fraud with aggressive quantization and a tuned larger model for chat. The runtime supports model variants and automatic fallbacks if capacity is constrained - e.g., route to a 7B-compatible variant if 13B is overloaded. Note though that fallbacks can impact quality, so we can set strict routing policies if quality is mandatory.
[07:16] Sonia: curious about multi-region. We need us-west primary but fall back to us-east during outages. How does cross-region routing affect latency?
[07:24] Liam: cross-region will add network RTT; for fraud if you need sub-300ms p95 you should keep inference in the same region. For failover we can have warm capacity in another region or smaller cold pools with automatic routing; warm capacity increases cost but reduces failover latency.
[07:42] Carlos: right. Also our SRE wants to run an in-house benchmark on Private deployment later. How different are the numbers between Private and Dedicated?
[07:52] Liam: Private gives you same control as Dedicated but network and infra differences matter - on-prem GPUs can have different interconnect and kernel support. Our internal kernels and compilation try to make performance consistent, but you'll need an on-site benchmark. For Dedicated we manage the infra so numbers are more predictable.
[08:10] Sonia: we heard quantization sometimes hurts accuracy for fraud models - any risk?
[08:16] Liam: quantization can change model behavior; we recommend running your regression evals (we can run eval harness against your prompt set) to measure quality delta. For fraud, even small changes can affect thresholds, so often teams keep unquantized for fraud and quantize chat models where quality impact is acceptable.
[08:35] Carlos: ok let's talk benchmarking specifics - can you run a 1k request run at a few concurrency levels? For fraud: 50, 100, 200. For chat streaming: 50, 200, 400 active. Capture p50/p95/p99, mean inter-token spacing, TTFB, tokens/sec aggregated.
[08:53] Liam: yes we can. We'll run both Hosted and Dedicated variants if you want to compare. We'll also test with and without prefix caching and with quantized model variants.
[09:06] Maya: we'll need the prompt set and an S3 link or secure upload; Evan can provide that. Also we'll need to know whether test traffic should exit via your VPC or hosted internet.
[09:17] Evan: we'll upload sample prompts to S3 and give you an IAM role for read-only. Prefer tests from within our VPC for latency realism - is there a test harness you recommend?
[09:26] Liam: we have a benchmark runner that can run inside your VPC or from our infra; best is within VPC to account for networking. We'll provide a small container or K6 script.
[09:36] Carlos: what about tokenization differences between models affecting perceived tokens/sec?
[09:40] Liam: yeah tokenization matters; we'll normalize by reporting tokens according to the model tokenizer and report characters/sec too if helpful.
[09:48] Sonia: any gotchas on streaming SDKs? Our product team wants websockets + chunked responses and function-calling when appropriate.
[09:57] Liam: streaming is supported via websocket or SSE; we also support function/tool calling for structured outputs. For smooth UI behavior we recommend chunk buffering and server flush intervals. We'll share SDK examples.
[10:10] Carlos: please include the streaming SDK example in your follow-up.
[10:14] Maya: will do - include links to the streaming SDK and a sample chunking config.
[10:20] Evan: ok on the security doc - we need to validate the KMS flow. For Dedicated can you ensure keys are customer-side?
[10:27] Liam: for Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS so keys are in your account; for Private it's fully customer-managed. We'll include an architecture diagram in the security pack.
[10:35] Carlos: about SLAs - what p95 uptime do you guarantee?
[10:38] Maya: Dedicated comes with SLA options; typical service uptime SLA is 99.9% with latency SLOs per route configurable as part of the contract. We'll send the SLA terms.
[10:48] Sonia: can you show an example of per-route latency budgets in the console?
[10:52] Liam: yes, per-route SLOs and tracing are visible in Redwood Console; you can set canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies. We'll share a short demo recording.
[11:05] Carlos: let's talk numbers for sizing: if we need to support 400 active streaming generations at 30 tokens/sec perceived, what aggregate tokens/sec is that?
[11:13] Liam: 400 * 30 = 12k tokens/sec perceived. Accounting for overhead and network jitter, aim for ~15k tokens/sec capacity. With model choice and quantization that maps to GPU pool sizes - we'll run the test to get exact GPU count and then map to Dedicated commit.
[11:30] Maya: I'll note that mapping: 15k tokens/sec target for streaming.
[11:34] Carlos: and for fraud 200 concurrent at average 180 tokens total per request (in+out) at, say, 99 req/s peak equals ~17.8k tokens/sec? hmm math check - I think we should just rely on your sizing calc.
[11:50] Liam: yeah we'll run exact numbers in the cost model.
[11:54] Evan: one more operational: how do we do deployments and rollouts? We want canary for model updates.
[11:59] Liam: Redwood supports canary rollouts and A/B routing by model version; you can route a percent of traffic to new model and do automatic rollback on latency or quality regressions.
[12:12] Sonia: are we able to run evals on every candidate model release?
[12:15] Liam: yes our eval tooling integrates with your prompt sets and can run quality/regression tests; we'll include that in the POC plan.
[12:25] Carlos: ok excellent. Next steps recap?
[12:29] Maya: recap: A) Evan to upload prompt set + IAM by 2026-03-06; B) Liam to run Hosted + Dedicated benchmarks (with/without cache/quant) and post results by 2026-03-09; C) Maya to send pricing, SLA, and SOC2/security pack by 2026-03-05; D) schedule Private deep-dive 2026-03-11.
[12:50] Sonia: sounds good. Anything else?
[12:53] Carlos: just one quick Q - if benchmark fails to meet p95, what alternatives?
[12:58] Liam: options: increase Dedicated capacity (reserve more GPUs), switch fraud to smaller special-purpose models, use more aggressive caching, or accept slightly higher p95 and implement client-side timeouts/fallbacks. We'll propose a few capacity/price combos based on results.
[13:16] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and links. Links referenced: Benchmark sheet: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/aether-2026-03-04 (private), Pricing deck: https://redwood.app/sales/decks/aether-pricing.pdf, Streaming SDK examples: https://redwood.app/docs/streaming-sdk
[13:36] (end of recorded portion)

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had a few mis-heard terms (e.g., "K-V cash" instead of "KV cache" in one spot, saw occasional speaker label swaps).
